## Recap from Last Two Classes {.smaller}

- We've been observing people out in the world, in their natural state
- We want to know effects of programs for people who chose to participate
- We use people who did not participate as comparison group, to estimate participants' counterfactuals
  - But factors that cause participation & also affect outcomes create selection bias
</ul><li class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1">Covariate-based strategies of regression adjustment & matching help reduce selection bias</li>
  <ul class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1">
  <li>But will not eliminate it unless there are no unmeasured confounders</li>
  <li>Impossible to know</li>
  </ul>
<li class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2">DiD limits the type of unmeasured confounders that can cause selection bias</li>
  <ul class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2">
  <li>And gives us a way to check the likelihood that these are present & giving us serious problems</li>
  <li>...but still can't guarantee that we've eliminated them</li>
  </ul>

# Randomized <br>Controlled Trials

## Random Assignment <br>Eliminates Selection Bias

- **Randomized controlled trials**: design defined by the use of **random assignment**
  - Randomly choose from a group of people who will participate in the program
- Those not randomly selected become the comparison group
  - "Control" group[^fn-ctrl-group]
- Random assignment can ***guarantee the elimination of selection bias***
  - Making RCTs the strongest / most internally valid design

[^fn-ctrl-group]: In practice, comparison groups are usually referred to as the "control" group, even in quasi-experimental designs like DiD

## How Does Random Assignment <br>Eliminate Selection Bias? {.smaller}

## Random Assignment in Action

```{r}
set.seed(6)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
data <- data.frame(
  participate = rep(c(1,0), each = 250)
) |>
  mutate(
    group = ifelse(participate == 1, 'participant', 'comparison'),
    test_score = rnorm(500, 100, 25) + participate * 30,
    income = rnorm(500, 75, 25) + participate * 20,
    age = rnorm(500, 12, 2) + participate,
    prek = c(rep(1, 150), rep(0, 100), rep(1, 75), rep(0, 175)),
    red = c(rep(1, 200), rep(0, 50), rep(1, 25), rep(0, 225)),
    blue = c(rep(0, 200), rep(1, 50), rep(0, 25), rep(1, 225)),
    y0 = test_score + income * .1 + age * 2 + prek * 5 + red
  )

# hand the data to the interactive pieces below (Observable JS)
ojs_define(ra_data = data)
```

```{ojs}
// participate as R made it: first 250 participants, last 250 comparison
ra_natural = transpose(ra_data).map(d => d.participate)

// blur so the arrow keys / space keep moving the slides after a click
ra_blur = () => document.activeElement?.blur()

// Randomize shuffles who participates (still 250 per group); Reset puts
// back the original assignment
viewof ra_assign = Inputs.button([
  ["randomize", () => { ra_blur(); return d3.shuffle(ra_natural.slice()) }],
  ["reset to natural", () => { ra_blur(); return ra_natural }]
], {value: ra_natural})
```

```{ojs}
// data with the current assignment: participate and group follow it,
// everything else stays with the person
ra_current = transpose(ra_data).map((d, i) => ({
  ...d,
  participate: ra_assign[i],
  group: ra_assign[i] === 1 ? "participant" : "comparison"
}))

ra_vars = Object.keys(ra_data).filter(v => !["participate", "group"].includes(v))
```

```{ojs}
// means of each variable by group
ra_mean = (v, p) => d3.mean(ra_current.filter(d => d.participate === p), d => d[v])

// how each variable's mean is shown (the 0/1 variables as percentages)
ra_fmt = {
  const pct = v => `${Math.round(v * 100)}%`
  return {
    test_score: v => v.toFixed(0),
    income: v => `$${v.toFixed(0)}k`,
    age: v => v.toFixed(1),
    prek: pct,
    red: pct,
    blue: pct,
    y0: v => v.toFixed(0)

}

// name shown for each variable
ra_labels = ({
  test_score: "Base Test Score",
  income: "Fam Income",
  age: "Age",
  prek: "Did Pre-K",
  red: "Red",
  blue: "Blue",

})

html`<div class="ra-means"><table>

  <tbody>${ra_vars.map(v => html`<tr class=${v === "y0" ? "ra-y0" : null}>
    <td>${ra_labels[v]}</td><td>${ra_fmt[v](ra_mean(v, 1))}</td><td>${ra_fmt[v](ra_mean(v, 0))}</td>
  </tr>`)}</tbody>
</table></div>`
```

```{ojs}
// full data table, collapsed until the full data button is clicked.
// participate is left out to save space (group shows the same thing)
ra_full_cols = Object.keys(ra_data).filter(v => v !== "participate")

// built once each time it's opened; ra_full.update() then rewrites the
// cells in place when the data changes, rather than redrawing the table
// (which flickers and loses the scroll position)
ra_full = {
  if (!ra_show_full) return html``
  const fmt = x => typeof x === "number" && !Number.isInteger(x) ? x.toFixed(1) : x
  const rows = transpose(ra_data).map(() => ra_full_cols.map(() => html`<td></td>`))
  const el = html`<div class="ra-full"><table>
    <thead><tr>${ra_full_cols.map(v => html`<th>${v}</th>`)}</tr></thead>
    <tbody>${rows.map(cells => html`<tr>${cells}</tr>`)}</tbody>
  </table></div>`
  el.update = data => data.forEach((d, i) => ra_full_cols.forEach((v, j) => {
    rows[i][j].textContent = fmt(d[v])
  }))
  return el
}
```

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{ojs}
// one person icon per row of the data, colored by red / blue, in a block
// per group 15 across (the biggest icons that fill the slide's height:
// 17 rows, the last one partial). built once; ra_people.update() moves
// them afterwards so the moves animate (styles in style_8.css)
ra_people = {
  const people = transpose(ra_data)
  const wrap = html`<div class="ra-people">
    <div class="ra-head" style="left: 0%">Participant</div>
    <div class="ra-head" style="left: 54%">Comparison</div>
  </div>`
  const icons = people.map(d => {
    const el = html`<div class="ra-person">${svg`<svg viewBox="0 0 20 40" fill=${d.red === 1 ? "#EE1289" : "#00B2EE"}>
      <circle cx="10" cy="6" r="5.5"/>
      <path d="M5 13h10a3 3 0 0 1 3 3v11h-3.5v12h-3.5v-11h-2v11h-3.5v-12h-3.5v-11a3 3 0 0 1 3-3z"/>
    </svg>`}</div>`
    wrap.append(el)
    return el
  })

  // each person's spot: their group (p) and position within its block
  const count = {1: 0, 0: 0}
  const natural = people.map(d => ({p: d.participate, pos: count[d.participate]++}))
  let spots = natural.map(s => ({...s}))
  const place = (el, s) => {
    el.style.left = `${(s.p === 1 ? 0 : 54) + (s.pos % 15) * (46 / 15)}%`
    el.style.top = `${45 + Math.floor(s.pos / 15) * 33}px`
  }

  // reset puts everyone back in their original spot. otherwise each group
  // fills reds from the top and blues below them. people who stay in their
  // group keep their spot if it's still in their color's zone, and
  // everyone else (switchers, plus stayers whose zone moved) takes the
  // first free spot in their zone, so as few people move as possible
  wrap.update = assign => {
    if (assign === ra_natural) {
      spots = natural.map(s => ({...s}))
    } else {
      for (const g of [1, 0]) {
        const members = people.map((d, i) => i).filter(i => assign[i] === g)
        const nRed = members.filter(i => people[i].red === 1).length
        const zone = i => people[i].red === 1 ? [0, nRed] : [nRed, members.length]
        const inZone = (i, pos) => pos >= zone(i)[0] && pos < zone(i)[1]
        const taken = new Set()
        const stay = members.filter(i => spots[i].p === g && inZone(i, spots[i].pos))
        stay.forEach(i => taken.add(spots[i].pos))
        members.filter(i => !stay.includes(i)).forEach(i => {
          let pos = zone(i)[0]
          while (taken.has(pos)) pos++
          taken.add(pos)
          spots[i] = {p: g, pos}
        })
      }
    }
    spots.forEach((s, i) => place(icons[i], s))
  }

  spots.forEach((s, i) => place(icons[i], s))
  return wrap
}
```

```{ojs}
//| output: false
ra_people.update(ra_assign)
```

## RCT: Difference in Mean Outcomes = <br>Unbiased Prog Effect Estimate

- After random assignment:
  - Participant Avg Baseline Vars $\approx$ Comparison Avg Baseline Vars
  - Participant Avg $Y(0) \approx$ Comparison Avg $Y(0)$
  - Prog Effect $\approx$ Participant Avg $Y -$ Comparison Avg $Y$

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 style="display: flex; justify-content: center;"}
🌟🥇🏆 ***"Gold standard" design*** 🏆🥇🌟
:::

<ul><li class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2">Useful to combine with covariate adjustment to help reduce noise from chance baseline imbalance</li>
<ul class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2"><li>Especially using a baseline measure of the outcome</li></ul></ul>

## RCT Validity Threat 1: Attrition {.smaller}

- Inevitably, people will **attrit**: drop out of the study or be unreachable at follow-up
- Their ***data is missing***
- **Differential attrition**: when groups have different attrition rates, this can ***create selection bias***

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
data <- data.frame(
  participate = rep(c(1, 0), each = 100),
  group = rep(c('Participant', 'Control'), each = 100)
) |>
  mutate(
    y = rnorm(200, 20, 5) + participate * 3
  ) |>
  # the lowest scorers in each group are missing: 10 participants, 30 controls
  mutate(.by = group, miss = as.integer(rank(y) <= if_else(participate == 1, 10, 45)))

# each group's points with a big point at its mean. drop_missing grays out
# the people with miss == 1 and leaves them out of the means. the jitter
# has a fixed seed, so the points sit in the same spots in both versions
attrition_plot <- function(drop_missing) {
  d <- data |>
    mutate(
      group = factor(group, levels = c("Participant", "Control")),
      color = if_else(drop_missing & miss == 1, "missing", as.character(group))
    )
  means <- d |>
    filter(!(drop_missing & miss == 1)) |>
    summarise(.by = group, y = mean(y))
  diff <- means$y[means$group == "Participant"] - means$y[means$group == "Control"]
  ggplot(d, aes(group, y, color = color)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7, position = position_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0, seed = 1)) +
    # line between the means, with the difference written above it. the
    # label starts just right of the participants and runs out over the
    # control group, above its highest point (the same spot in both versions)
    geom_line(data = means, aes(group = 1), color = "black") +
    annotate(
      "text", x = 1.3, y = max(d$y[d$group == "Control"]) + 6, hjust = 0, size = 6,
      label = paste0("Participant \u2212 Control = ", sprintf("%.1f", diff))
    ) +
    geom_point(data = means, size = 4.5, color = "black") +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(
      Participant = "deepskyblue2", Control = "deeppink2", missing = "gray"
    )) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Post-Prog Test") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "none"
    )
}
```

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}

## RCT Validity Threat 2: Consent

- Finding people who consent to being in RCTs is a big challenge
  - Consent rates frequently well below 50%
- Mostly an external validity issue: can ***only learn about effects for population of people willing to consent***
- But if ***randomization is done prior to consent***, this creates potential for ***differential consent***
  - This can ***create selection bias*** in the same way as differential attrition
  - "Waitlist control" designs may face this (ask me how I know...😓)

## Intent-to-Treat vs. <br>Treatment-on-the-Treated {.smaller #itt-tot}

- Some people assigned to a program don't do it
  - And some who are not assigned will do it anyway
- **Intent-to-treat (ITT)**: effect of being ***assigned to a program***
- **Treatment-on-the-treated (TOT)**: effect of actually ***doing the program***[^fn-cace]
<li class=fragment data-fragment-index="1">ITT is the straightforward estimate:</li></ul>

[$ITT =Y_{\textit{assigned to particiate}} - Y_{\textit{assigned to control}}$]{.fragment fragment-index=1}

<ul class=fragment data-fragment-index="2"><li>But all effects come from just the subset who actually participate (and wouldn't have if assigned to control)</li>
  <ul><li>So the effect of participation must be larger than ITT</li></ul></ul>

[$TOT = \frac{ITT}{\textit{% induced to participate}}$ &emsp; [see appendix for details](#appendix-tot){style="font-size: 0.7em;"}]{.fragment fragment-index=2}

[^fn-cace]: Another name for TOT is complier average causal effect (CACE). I like CACE better but it's more technical so we'll stick with TOT for class.

## Unit of Assignment

- **Individual** assignment: assign individual people (or whatever your unit of analysis) to program or control
- **Cluster** assignment: assign entire clusters of people/units to program or control
  - Example: entire schools of students are assigned to either participate or not
- Cluster-randomized typically requires a large number of clusters (eg schools) to participate in study for adequate statistical power

## Treatment Contrast {.smaller}

- **Treatment contrast**: difference between what the ***control group gets*** and what the program group gets
  - **Counterfactual condition**: the services/conditions for the control group
- "**Business as usual**": most common counterfactual condition, where control group gets whatever services they would typically get
  - These "business as usual" conditions can vary from place-to-place or over time
  - This variation can have big implications on the estimated program effects
- Example: effect of Head Start
  - If most children in the community can already access free high-quality pre-k, the effect may be small
  - But if most children are unable to access pre-k, the effect may be large
- Many different types of treatment contrasts can be set up; each answers a different evaluation question

# Regression Discontinuity

## Example for RD Intuition

- Students must all take a placement test; if they score below 180, they must take a remedial course
- We want to know the effect of the remedial course on main course performance
- We can use a **regression discontinuity** (RD) design:
  - Participant group: students who ***scored 179***
  - Control group: students who ***scored 180***
- These students are ***basically the same***, with just 1 point difference
- So any difference in course performance we observe should be due to the remedial course rather than confounders

## RD Takes Advantage of <br>"Assignment Variables" {.smaller}

- **Assignment variable**:[^fn-assign-var] variable that assigns people to program
- **Cutoff**:[^fn-cutoff] the point on the assignment variable where...
  - People with values below are assigned to one group (eg program)
  - People with values above are assigned to the other group (eg control)

[^fn-assign-var]: Also called "running" or "forcing" variable
[^fn-cutoff]: Also called "cut point", "cut score", or "threshold"

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 1.9
#| fig-align: center
# number line of the assignment variable, split at the cutoff

# curly brace from x1 to x2, hanging down from y with its point h below:
# two sigmoids per half give the curled ends and the point in the middle
brace <- function(x1, x2, y, h, k = 25) {
  u <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 100)
  half <- 1 / (1 + exp(-k * u)) + 1 / (1 + exp(-k * (u - 1))) - 0.5
  data.frame(x = x1 + (x2 - x1) * c(u, 1 + u[-1]) / 2,
    y = y - h * c(half, rev(half)[-1]))
}
arrow_head <- arrow(length = unit(0.1, "in"))
# 10 dashes from y = -0.95 to 0.95, with gaps the same length as the dashes
cut_len <- (0.95 - -0.95) / (2 * 10 - 1)
cut_dash <- seq(-0.95, 0.95 - cut_len, by = 2 * cut_len)

ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = 135, xend = 225, y = 0, yend = 0, linewidth = 1) +
  # x-axis style ticks every 10 points
  annotate("segment", x = seq(140, 220, 10), xend = seq(140, 220, 10), y = 0, yend = -0.15) +
  annotate("text", x = seq(140, 220, 10), y = -0.45, label = seq(140, 220, 10), size = 6) +
  # the cutoff: dashed line drawn as separate dashes, sized so it starts
  # and ends on a full dash
  annotate("segment", x = 180, xend = 180, y = cut_dash, yend = cut_dash + cut_len,
    linewidth = 1, lineend = "butt") +
  # braces under the scores on each side of the cutoff, labeled at their points
  geom_path(data = brace(136, 179.5, -0.75, 0.3), aes(x, y), color = "deepskyblue2") +
  geom_path(data = brace(180.5, 224, -0.75, 0.3), aes(x, y), color = "deeppink2") +
  annotate("text", x = c(157.75, 202.25), y = -1.35, size = 7,
    label = c("remedial course", "no remedial course"), color = c("deepskyblue2", "deeppink2")) +
  annotate("text", x = 169.5, y = 0.6, label = "cutoff", size = 7, fontface = "italic") +
  annotate("segment", x = 174, xend = 179.3, y = 0.55, yend = 0.35, arrow = arrow_head) +
  # title of the line
  annotate("text", x = 180, y = 1.3, label = "Assignment Variable: Placement Test Score",
    size = 7, fontface = "bold") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1.62, 1.55)) +
  theme_void()
```

<ul><li class=fragment data-fragment-index="1">Assignment to program is "***as good as random***" if we know people's assignment variable value</li></ul>

## RD Effect = Size of "Discontinuity" {.smaller}

- Program assignment based on cutoff score creates ***"discontinuity" in the relationship*** between ***assignment variable & outcome***
- RD effect estimate = size of the discontinuity = diff btwn those just below & above cutoff

```{r}
set.seed(6)
data <- tibble::tibble(
  placement_test = rnorm(300, 190, 30),
  below_180 = ifelse(placement_test < 180, 1, 0),
  y = pmin(15 + placement_test * .3 + rnorm(300, 5, 2), 100),
  y_rd = y + 10 * below_180
)
```

:::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r}
ggplot(data, aes(placement_test, y)) + 
  geom_point(color = 'deeppink2', alpha = .5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "deeppink4", linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(140, 180, 220, 260)) +
  # oob_keep: the fitted lines run slightly past 100 at the top end; keep
  # them going instead of cutting them off where they cross the limit
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(50, 100, 10), limits = c(min(data$y), 100),
    oob = scales::oob_keep) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Placement Test Score", y = "Course Grade") +
  ggtitle("Natural Relationship Between Placement Test and Course Grade")
```

## RD Effects Are "Local" to <br>People At the Cutoff {.smaller}

- RD estimates effects ***only for people just below & above*** the cutoff
- **Local average treatment effect** (LATE): the effect is "local" to people with these assignment variable scores
- ***Effects may be different*** for people with ***different values on the assignment variable***
- For instance, in our example:

$$
Prog \: Effect_{RD} = Y_{place \: test = 179} - Y_{place \: test = 180}
$$

- But people who scored eg 160 on the placement test may have benefitted less (or more) from the remedial course
- ***RD cannot tell us about the effects for people who scored far from the cutoff*** on the placement test

## Biggest Threat to Validity: <br>Manipulation at the Cutoff

- Someone may ***know about the cutoff*** and ***intentionally try to score higher or lower*** to get into (or out of) the program
- Introduces ***selection bias***, as ***people are now "choosing"*** whether to do the program, ***rather than their score "assigning"*** them
- Check for **bunching** to see if this might be happening

## Bunching Check

- Look at a histogram, which shows the number of people at each assignment variable value
- Many more scores just to one side of the cutoff than the other = evidence of manipulation

:::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
set.seed(6)
data_bunch <- tibble::tibble(
  placement_test = rnorm(10000, 210, 30),
  placement_test_bunch = ifelse(
    placement_test < 180 & placement_test > 177, placement_test + 2, placement_test
  )
) |> 
  filter(placement_test > 141 & placement_test < 279)
ggplot(data_bunch) +
  geom_histogram(aes(placement_test), color = 'deepskyblue4', binwidth = 2, fill = 'deepskyblue2') +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 179), lty = "dashed") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = .5)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(160, 180, 200, 220, 240, 260)) +
  ggtitle('No Bunching') +
  xlab('Placement Test Score')
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

## Covariate Discontinuities = <br>Possible Selection Bias

- If there are ***discontinuities in covariates at the cutoff***, the groups are ***imbalanced***
  - These covariates will ***create selection bias*** if they affect outcome
- Check for this by:
  - Plotting the relationships between the assignment variable & baseline covariates
  - Estimating the "effect" of the assignment var on the covariate, as if it was the outcome; large estimates are sign of trouble

## RD Estimation Requires Modeling <br>Relationship Btwn Assign Var & Outcome {.smaller}

- Conceptually, RD is difference between those just below and above the cutoff
- But we typically don't have enough observations *just* below & above
- So we estimate the relationship between assign var & outcome on both sides of cutoff
- RD effect estimate = gap between the relationship lines at the cutoff

::: {style="display: flex; justify-content: center"}
```{r}

#| fig-height: 4

  geom_point(alpha = .5) +
  # separate lines below and above the cutoff, in darker shades of their dots' colors
  geom_smooth(aes(color = paste0("line", below_180)), method = "lm", formula = y ~ x,
    se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`1` = "deepskyblue2", `0` = "deeppink2",
    line1 = "deepskyblue4", line0 = "deeppink4"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(140, 180, 220, 260)) +
  # oob_keep: the fitted lines run slightly past 100 at the top end; keep
  # them going instead of cutting them off where they cross the limit
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(50, 100, 10), limits = c(min(data$y), 100),
    oob = scales::oob_keep) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Placement Test Score", y = "Course Grade") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 180), lty = "dashed")
```
:::

## Bandwidth: <br>How Far From the Cutoff Do We Go? {.smaller}

- The ***further we get from cutoff***, the ***more different people become***
  - And thus the ***more we rely on statistical estimation*** to get relationship for people near cutoff
- So we ***limit our sample to those within a certain distance*** from cutoff, aka **bandwidth**

:::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r}

#| fig-height: 4

  # oob_keep: the fitted lines run slightly past 100 at the top end; keep
  # them going instead of cutting them off where they cross the limit
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(50, 100, 10), limits = c(min(data$y), 100),
    oob = scales::oob_keep) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
```

## The Smaller the Bandwidth, the <br>Smaller the Sample...

- ...and therefore the ***less statistical power*** we have
- So there's always a ***tradeoff*** with bandwidth: ***internal validity vs. precision***

:::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}

# Comparing Strategies

## Non-Randomized vs. Controlled & <br>External vs. Internal Validity {.smaller}

- ***Non-randomized*** strategies (covariate-based, DiD) ***observe the world as it naturally occurs***
  - Therefore, they often have ***higher external validity***
  - But they ***can't control who accesses program***, so have ***lower internal validity***
- ***Controlled*** strategies (RCT, RD) ***assign people*** to program & comparison groups
  - They have ***higher internal validity*** due to this control
  - But ***RCTs are unnatural*** scenarios, so they may have ***lower external validity***
  - And ***RD*** only estimates ***effects for those near cutoff***, so they also may have ***lower external validity***

# Appendix

## "Scale Up" the ITT Estimate to <br>Get TOT {.parens .smaller #appendix-tot}

[back to main slide](#itt-tot){style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

- All effects must come from those assigned to participate who
  (a) Actually participated
  (b) Wouldn't have participated if assigned to control
- ***Otherwise, potential outcomes are the same*** regardless of assignment
- So the difference in outcomes should be ***averaged across just this subset of people***, rather than the whole participant group

:::: {.columns .fragment fragment-index=1}
::: {.column .center-table width="50%"}

| assignment | participated |
|---|---|
| participate | 70% |
| control | 20% |

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

% "treated" $= 70\% - 20\% = 50\%$

[TOT $= \frac{ITT}{0.50}$]{.fragment fragment-index=2}

[So if ITT is, for example, 10:]{.fragment fragment-index=3}

[TOT $= \frac{10}{0.50} = 20$]{.fragment fragment-index=3}

:::
::::
